title: On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents

paper.title: On the Clock: Towards Punctual and Productive Time-Budgeted AI Agents
paper.abstract: Abstract We study whether small LLM agents can operate effectively under explicit wall-clock time budgets by both respecting the allocated runtime and using available time productively. We evaluate Qwen3.6-27B on five competitions from MLE-Bench Lite and Qwen3-4B on Zork I (Jericho), two agentic benchmarks where additional computational time can meaningfully improve performance. In the simplest setting, where the budget is stated only in the prompt, agents fail to translate the stated budget into controlled use of time. These failures arise from gaps in time awareness, since the harness provides no timing feedback, but also because they cannot reliably anticipate the duration of actions, and do not have a learned mapping from available time to an appropriate strategy. We investigate two complementary classes of interventions: harness-based mechanisms that expose timing information and enforce deadlines, and reinforcement learning with budget-aware rewards. Injecting timing information through the harness substantially improves budget adherence for Qwen3.6-27B without measurable loss in performance, while enforcement hooks tighten adherence further. RL with GRPO achieves near-perfect budget adherence on Zork I and generalizes to held-out budgets not seen during training, but does not improve task performance over the untrained harness on MLE-Bench. Once agents are made to respect the budget, they still fail to use additional time to improve task performance. RL-trained policies learn when to stop but often fill extra time with repeated actions, and GRPO training on multiple budgets tends to collapse toward the strategy learned for the shortest budget. Our results reveal a gap between time adherence and productive time allocation, which remains a central challenge for budget-conditioned agents.

Color gives the stated budget and dashed lines mark the budget values. (Right two) Mid-episode time estimation on 15-minute MLE-Bench tasks. The agent is asked how long it has been working and how long the run will take in total, and its answer is plotted against the true value, with the dashed diagonal marking a perfect estimate. Open markers have a clock in context, filled markers do not. As AI agents take on complex, long-horizon tasks involving planning, tool use, and iterative refinement, how long they spend on a task becomes an important dimension of their behavior, alongside the quality of the final solution. Agents should be able to operate effectively under explicit wall-clock time budgets for two reasons. First, agents face external constraints . A user should be able to control how long a task takes end to end, and an agent embedded in a larger system must meet deadlines to coordinate with other components. Second, for many tasks time is aligned with quality . In search-heavy problems such as ML engineering, more time allows an agent to explore more architectures, hyperparameters, or candidate solutions, so making agents as fast as possible is not the goal. At the same time, users differ in how they weigh solution quality against time, and a time budget is how a user expresses that trade-off. We require two things from an agent operating under a budget, which we call adherence and productive use . Adherence means the agent returns a solution within the allocated time; a harness can force this with a hard interrupt, so that the agent works to the deadline itself. Productive use means the agent spends that time well, using additional budget to improve the solution rather than stopping early or padding its runtime with unnecessary actions. A concrete test is whether task performance improves as the budget increases. If the agent achieves the same quality under a tight budget as under a generous one, the additional time is not being converted into a better solution. Much of these tasks are also dominated by tool call latencies, and we test how well the model is able to take in both the latencies and its generation time in order to stay in budget. Current agents fail at adherence even in the simplest setting, where the budget is stated in the prompt and the harness gives no feedback on elapsed time. On MLE-Bench, Qwen3.6-27B does not use the allocated time effectively (Figure 1 , left; Table 1 ). Qwen3.6-27B runs for roughly ten minutes regardless of the stated budget, overrunning an 8-minute budget while using a small fraction of a 60-minute budget. These failures reflect concrete gaps in what the model can observe and predict about time. Nothing in the model’s context indicates elapsed wall-clock time, and token count is a poor proxy since it depends on hardware and inference configuration. Probing the models directly confirms this. Asked mid-episode how long it has been working, Qwen3.6 27b misjudges its own elapsed time by a large amount on a 15-minute task (Figure 1 , right; Table 9 , Appendix). Agents also cannot reliably predict how long their actions will take, which matters most for long-running tool calls such as training jobs, and even with a clock in context, forecasts of the run’s remaining and total duration stay far off. We hypothesize that even an agent with perfect timing information must still learn to map available time to an appropriate plan. We investigate two complementary classes of interventions: harness-based and learning-based. Harness-based interventions close the observational gaps. A per-action clock and periodic reminders report the remaining budget and the time cost of each action, and an enforcement mode optionally holds the deadline by clamping or refusing over-long commands. Learning-based interventions target the planning gap. We also explore reinforcement learning (GRPO) against budget-aware rewards as a preliminary step toward internalizing the time–quality trade-off directly. We evaluate on two agentic settings where additional time can meaningfully improve outcomes, five competitions from MLE-Bench Lite and Zork I (Jericho), which differ in action structure, feedback density, and how time converts into quality. We select a small number of tasks where different budgets should favor different strategies, and analyze failure modes in detail. In this work, we separate the problem of time budgeting into adherence and productive use, two parts of very different difficulty. We show that adherence is largely solvable in our settings. The harness brings Qwen3.6-27B from 161 % 161\% of budget to on-budget with no measurable loss in quality (between the runs with and without the harness), and RL yields near-exact adherence on Zork I that generalizes to held-out budgets, though training is less effective on MLE-Bench, where the search space is much larger. Productive use , however, is much harder. We show that agents that stay on time do not convert additional time into better outcomes, and the RL policy that learns when to stop fills extra time with actions that do not produce better task results. 2 Related Work Budget-awareness and time-aware test-time scaling. Lin et al. [ 1 ] formalize budget-awareness as progressive interval estimation, where the agent predicts upper and lower bounds on remaining budget at each step, and find that frontier agents are consistently over-optimistic about how much budget remains. Their SFT+RL training improves early-stop behavior, but precise calibration remains difficult. Our work focuses on wall-clock time rather than token budgets, and studies the progression from prompting through harness enforcement to RL rather than a single training method. Li et al. [ 2 ] propose a training-free Budget-Aware Value Tree Search that shifts from exploration to exploitation as budget depletes, and McCleary and Ghawaly [ 3 ] measure how search depth, retrieval strategy, and completion budget affect accuracy under fixed constraints. Both operate at the token or tool-call level. We study wall-clock time, whose stochastic action durations token counting cannot capture. Snell et al. [ 4 ] show that a compute-optimal test-time scaling strategy can outperform a 14 × 14\times larger model, but assume an unlimited budget. Ma et al. [ 5 ] redefine test-time scaling in wall-clock terms with the Timely-Eval benchmark and a Timely-RL training method, and find that existing models fail to adapt reasoning to time budgets. Where Ma et al. focus on a single RL intervention, we compare prompting, harness enforcement, and RL as a progression. Paglieri et al. [ 6 ] use SFT and RL to teach agents when planning is worthwhile. We study how the entire strategy should adapt to a time budget, and find that RL learns when to stop but not what to do differently with more time. Budgeted and constrained reinforcement learning. Constrained Markov Decision Processes [ 7 ] formalize reward maximization subject to cost constraints. Carrara et al. [ 8 ] extend this to Budgeted MDPs, conditioning a single policy on the budget so it solves the CMDP for any budget level without retraining, an idea our RL stage adopts. Our cost signal, wall-clock time, is stochastic and unpredictable, while classical BMDPs assume known cost functions of state-action pairs. McMahan and Zhu [ 9 ] require that the budget never be violated at any point in time, closer to our setting since an agent that overruns at step t t cannot undo it at t + 1 t+1 . Their result that Markovian policies are insufficient under anytime constraints informs our choice to inject remaining budget into the agent’s context. Achille [ 10 ] argues that time is the critical quantity to optimize when scaling reasoning models, and warns of a failure mode in which reward-driven models brute-force solutions without acquiring transferable strategies. Our RL-trained policy’s memorized-prefix-plus-no-ops behavior matches this failure mode. Reinforcement learning for LLMs. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [ 11 ] , introduced for DeepSeek-Math and used for DeepSeek-R1 [ 12 ] , samples a group of rollouts per task and normalizes rewards within the group, avoiding a separate critic network. We adopt GRPO because this normalization handles the multi-modal reward distribution produced by training across several budget levels at once. 3 Setup 3.1 Datasets We evaluate time-budgeted agent behavior in two environments: machine learning engineering with MLE-Bench, and text-based games with Jericho Zork. We chose both because task performance scales meaningfully with wall-clock time, they admit multiple valid strategies at different budget levels, and they give graded scores for partially completed work. MLE-Bench Lite. MLE-Bench [ 13 ] evaluates agents on end-to-end machine learning tasks derived from Kaggle competitions. We use MLE-Bench Lite, a 22-competition subset, and select 5 tasks from it based on two criteria. The task must admit qualitatively different strategies at different time scales (e.g. a quick baseline versus iterative feature engineering), and preliminary runs must show non-trivial score variance across time budgets ranging from 10 to 25 minutes. Each task requires the agent to inspect data, develop and execute modeling code, iterate on experiments, and produce a valid submission. The environment is well suited for studying time-aware agents because additional wall-clock time enables different activities. A short budget may suffice for a single baseline model, while a longer budget allows time for data analysis, feature engineering, model selection, hyperparameter tuning, and longer training runs. We use a five-competition subset of MLE-Bench Lite, namely dog-breed identification and dogs-vs-cats (image classification), leaf classification (species classification from extracted leaf-image features), spooky-author identification (text classification), and NOMAD 2018 transparent-conductor prediction (tabular regression). We use Qwen3.6-27B [ 14 ] as the underlying language model, run through the OpenCode agentic harness. For RL training, we use an internal tool to obtain TITO (Training In, Training Out) formatted data from agent rollouts, converting trajectories into training samples for GRPO. We vary the wall-clock budget and measure how the agent’s trajectory and final task performance change as a function of available time. Jericho (Zork I). Jericho [ 15 ] is an interactive-fiction environment in which an agent interacts with a text-based game through natural-language actions. We use zork1 for all experiments. At each step the model observes the current game state, generates an action, and receives the resulting observation. Additional time translates directly into more exploration steps, and performance scales with how much of the world map the agent discovers and how many puzzles it solves along the way. For evaluations we use Qwen3-4B [ 14 ] , Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.8-27B [ 16 ] in a lightweight agentic loop with thinking mode off. The model repeatedly receives the observation, generates the next action, and observes the result until the trajectory terminates or the time budget is exhausted. We define the task reward, R task R_{\mathrm{task}} as the normalized game score, which provides a dense, comparable measure of progress across trajectories ( max ​ _ ​ score = 350 \mathrm{max\_score}=350 for Zork I). As shown by the Budget in Prompt rows in Table 6 , all models substantially overshoot the stated budget, often running until the hard cutoff at 2 × 2\times the budget terminates the episode (See Fig 2 .b). Task performance also remains near zero for most models. This behavior is expected: the models have no direct notion of wall-clock generation speed and receive no feedback about how much time has elapsed during execution. As a result, a stated budget provides a constraint in natural language, however out of the box models do not exhibit the ability to apply the constraint. 4.2 Interventions via Harness MLE-Bench. Exposing elapsed time through the harness made the agent substantially more responsive to its budget. Three hooks (Table 3 ) report the time remaining and the cost of generation, without prescribing any action. This reduced the time consumed from 161.4 % 161.4\% to 99.7 % 99.7\% of the stated budget, with no measurable change in quality ( 47.5 47.5 to 47.0 47.0 percentile, within error), and raised the fraction of runs producing a valid submission from 78 % 78\% to 88 % 88\% (Table 2 ). Hook When it fires What it does Per-tool clock After every tool call Adds the time remaining to the result the agent reads Periodic reminder On a fixed time interval Reports the time remaining even while a command is still running Generation accounting After every tool call Reports how long the model spent generating text before the action Enforcement (clamp) Before a shell command runs Shortens the command’s time limit so it stops by the deadline; the command still runs, but is cut off Enforcement (refuse) Before a shell command runs Blocks the command and returns a message explaining why, so the agent must choose something cheaper Table 3: Harness hooks. The first three only add information to what the agent reads. The two enforcement modes change the action itself and are never used together. The dominant failure mode was that when the agent recognized that little time remained, it launched a tool call whose duration exceeded that budget (for example a training with a timeout that is longer than the time remaining). Because the duration of a tool call is variable and hard to predict, the agent often had no further chance to act before it ran past the budget. Even when prompted to put tool calls in the background so it can interrupt the runs, the model is still unable to consistently stop in time. We therefore added an enforcement hook that inspects each shell command before it runs, comparing the time limit the agent set for the command against the time remaining. Because commands are frequently issued with no limit, a missing limit is treated as the harness default timeout. Enforcement cut the overrun further, at a small cost in quality. The on-time rate improved, while quality fell slightly. The quality cost is unsurprising, since the unenforced model was converting overrun time into score, and enforcement takes that time away. Shortening a command’s limit preserved most of the unenforced quality and produced the highest rate of valid submissions we measured ( 90 % 90\% ). Blocking commands outright held closer to the budget but reduced the valid formatted submission rate while increaseing interaction steps, because the agent reissued blocked commands with smaller limits. Even without RL training, the agent scales its elapsed time to the stated budget when given a clock. Figure 4 (Appendix) shows the time and quality distributions across four budgets. Quality is spread across the full percentile range at every budget, with no upward trend as budget grows. Zork I. To provide agents with an explicit sense of elapsed time, we introduce three harness-level interventions in Zork. First, the Clock Tool allows the model to issue a time_elapsed tool call, which returns a message of the form [time used: x x s of B B s budget] . Second, Clock Tool++ uses the same tool interface but provides substantially more guidance in the prompt on when and how to query it, together with an in-context example demonstrating its use. Third, the Auto-Clock harness removes the need for the model to actively request timing information after every interaction turn by having the harness automatically appends the same elapsed-time message to the context. The basic Clock Tool practically yields no improvements in adherence (See Fig 2 and Table 6 ). Even though the model now has access to wall-clock time, it must still decide when to query the tool, and models often fail to call it frequently enough for the feedback to be useful. Consequently, most models still continue to substantially overshoot short budgets. With Clock Tool++ , however, models invoke the tool much more often (Table 8 in Appendix), and the resulting increase in timing feedback leads to a comparatively better budget adherence. The strongest adherence comes from the Auto-Clock harness, where timing information is pushed into the context after every turn rather than being requested by the model. Under this intervention, most models track the available budget substantially more closely. However, a limitation is that harness feedback is only available between generations: if a single generation itself consumes a large fraction of the budget, the harness cannot intervene until that generation completes. This effect is particularly visible for larger models such as 9B and 27B. Another interesting observation is that the score remains below 5 5 across all budgets, despite substantially improved budget adherence. This suggests that access to time feedback helps the model determine when to stop , but does not teach it how to adapt its strategy . Therefore, we observe no meaningful score–budget trade-off in the frontier shown in Fig. 2 (a). 4.3 Interventions via RL Training 4.3.1 MLE-Bench Objective. We train with GRPO [ 11 ] . We select the step-wise reward for training our RL models. Although the shaped rewards exhibit broadly comparable behavior, step-wise provides the best overall balance between convergence speed, task score, and budget adherence (Table 7 ). We train the RL policies by sampling a time budget uniformly from 0 to 16s at each GRPO step and optimizing with the step-wise reward. We apply this training procedure to both the AutoClock and Clock Tool++ interventions and referring the resulting runs as RL + AutoClock and RL + Clock Tool++ , respectively. In both settings, the policies learn to remain within the allotted budget while also improving task performance under that budget and pushing the frontier (See Figure 2 (a)). However, RL + Clock Tool++ underperforms RL + AutoClock in score (Fig. 2 and Table 6 ). We attribute this gap to the overhead of active time checking since RL + Clock Tool++ spends roughly 50% of its turns querying the clock, leaving fewer actions for task progress. Despite this inefficiency, both policies achieve strong adherence, with generations typically terminating within ± 15 % \pm 15\% of the specified budget. Clock generalizes, the play doesn’t: We also train the same policy using discrete budgets rather than sampling uniformly from a continuous range, which allows us to study substantially longer horizons such as 15, 30, 60, and 90,s. Each rollout is assigned a budget from a predefined set we call budget mix, and the corresponding budget is provided to the model in the prompt. In principle, interleaving multiple budgets during training should encourage the policy to condition its behavior on the available time and use larger budgets for more extensive exploration. As training progresses, budget adherence becomes nearly perfect across the different horizons. However, the policy collapses toward the strategy learned for the smallest budget (Figure 3 ). Trajectories for different budgets separate cleanly in elapsed wall-clock time but their game scores follow nearly identical trends throughout training. In Zork, rollouts under different budgets open with the same memorized action sequence and reach the same score regardless of budget given. The budget changes only how long the episode is padded with filler actions before the agent quits. Mixed-budget training was intended to prevent this collapse, and it succeeded only at helping the model generalize stopping to multiple budgets. The same pattern holds on MLE-Bench, where extra time bought more attempts training models, but did not improve the final score. Also see Budget adherence through invalid actions . Memorization in fixed environments : Training on a single game with a fixed starting state makes memorization the cheapest path to higher score. The Zork policy converges on a recalled walkthrough prefix that collects a fixed number of points, after which no new score is found. When valid actions are fed back to the model instead of its own outputs, the same checkpoint scores far lower, confirming that the learned behavior does not survive even a small change. The reward structure compounds this problem by pricing elapsed time and not exploration, so once a scoring prefix exists, deviating from it offers no benefit. It also does not distinguish a rejected action from a productive one, and the trained policy fills remaining time by repeating a command. Budget utilization therefore only demonstrates the ability of the model to stop on time, but not on how well it used the allotted time. We discuss these mechanisms, and a third source of noise from stochastic action durations on MLE-Bench, in the Appendix. Scope of evaluation : Our experiments use two models (Qwen3-4B and Qwen3.6-27B) and two environments, and the RL experiments on Zork train on a single game. Whether the findings extend to frontier-scale models, to environments with richer strategy spaces remains open. The MLE-Bench subset contains five competitions, which limits the diversity of task structures the policy encounters during training. A broader evaluation across models, environment types, and task counts would strengthen the conclusions drawn here. 6 Conclusion We studied whether LLM agents can reason about and act under explicit time budgets, comparing two classes of interventions: (i) harness-based mechanisms that expose or enforce time information, and (ii) GRPO training that directly optimizes budget-conditioned behavior. Simply stating a time budget in the prompt is not sufficient: out-of-the-box agents struggle to estimate action durations, overshooting small budgets by up to 2 × 2\times on Zork and by 61 % 61\% on MLE-Bench. In contrast, exposing time through the agent harness substantially improves adherence. Informational clocks reduce overruns to near zero in both environments with little measurable loss in task quality, while stricter enforcement hooks tighten adherence further at a modest performance cost. GRPO training improves budget adherence further. On Zork, the trained policy matches the requested budget to within 0.2 0.2 s across budgets from 5 5 to 90 90 s, including four held-out budgets not seen during training. On MLE-Bench, trained policies consistently use between 0.87 0.87 and 0.93 0.93 of the allocated budget. At smaller budgets, RL also pushes the cost–score frontier outward, improving both adherence and task performance. However, this improvement does not extend uniformly to larger budgets. In these sparse-reward regimes, the current objectives provide little incentive for deeper exploration or qualitatively different strategies. On Zork, the policy converges to a fixed high-reward prefix and spends additional time on unproductive actions, causing score to saturate at 45 / 350 45/350 across larger budgets. Similarly on MLE-Bench, additional time similarly leads to more attempts at essentially the same training procedure without improving submission quality. We show that these results reveal a distinction between budget adherence and productive budget allocation (ability to change its behavior when given more time). These findings should be interpreted in light of three limitations: strategy collapse across budgets, memorization induced by fixed training environments and sparse rewards, and the limited scope of our evaluation across models and tasks. Possible directions include exploration-aware rewards that pay for novel states rather than elapsed time, environment variation that prevents memorization from substituting for search, and reward terms that distinguish repeated attempts from genuinely different strategies. The gap between adherence (which RL solves) and productive time allocation (which remains open) defines the central challenge for budget-conditioned agents. Appendix Reward structure and exploration incentives The reward is a function of final score and elapsed time only, so exploring is unpriced. In Zork, once a scoring prefix exists, deviation is actively risky. Our 4B models typically reach at most about 45 / 350 ≈ 0.129 45/350\approx 0.129 in score. With λ = 0.1 \lambda=0.1 , the time term is worth up to 0.100 0.100 , which is already comparable to the score term achieved by the policy. Moreover, because Zork rewards are relatively discrete, a meaningful improvement often requires gaining several additional points; gaining five more points, for example, increases the score term by only 5 / 350 ≈ 0.014 5/350\approx 0.014 . Perfect budget adherence is therefore worth about seven times as much as a genuine five-point discovery, and it is available deterministically from any token sequence that consumes the clock. Fixing this would require a term that pays for novelty (first-visit bonuses, walkthrough coverage, or potential-based shaping on distance to unreached states), together with environment variation across episodes so that recall cannot substitute for search. On MLE-Bench, the analogous problem is that the reward does not distinguish between repeated attempts at the same strategy and genuinely different approaches. A policy that submits the same baseline three times under a longer budget receives the same reward as one that tries progressively more sophisticated methods, as long as the best submission score is identical. Budget adherence through invalid actions Because the Zork time term is satisfied by wall-clock alone, the policy learns to consume the clock by emitting commands the parser rejects. In one particular training at step 500 the filler is the word forward , to which Zork replies I don’t know the word "forward". It appears in 127 127 of 128 128 rollouts, immediately after the memorized prefix ends, and accounts for 45 % 45\% of turns at B = 15 B=15 and 88 % 88\% of turns at B = 90 B=90 . The budget is met to within 0.2 0.2 s almost entirely through repetition of an action that advances nothing, since elapsed time measures wall-clock latency regardless of whether the action was accepted, and a rejected command consumes the same generation time as a valid move. This means “used 99 % 99\% of its budget” should not be read as 99 % 99\% of the budget spent working. Any claim about effort allocation requires a measure of useful time (turns that change game state, valid-command rate, or tokens spent on accepted actions). This failure mode is also easy to miss with the wrong diagnostic. Our repetition detector reports a trailing identical run of only 1.0 1.0 – 1.5 1.5 turns for these runs, because it measures the tail identical to the final action ( quit ), so hundreds of consecutive no-ops sit outside its window. Penalizing invalid actions or crediting only state-changing turns is a prerequisite for interpreting time-shaped rewards as effort. Comparing Reward Shapes Across the shaped variants, linear , Gaussian , and step perform comparably overall, suggesting that the precise shape of the time reward matters little once an explicit timing signal is present. The main difference is in budget matching. The step reward produces the most reliable adherence to the target budget, since it does not reward the model at all for being over budget. Action durations on MLE-Bench On MLE-Bench, action durations are stochastic and depend on factors outside the agent’s control (GPU availability, data loading, network latency). The same training script may take 30 30 seconds or 3 3 minutes depending on system load. This makes the reward noisy in a way that is uncorrelated with the agent’s decisions, complicating credit assignment during RL [ 9 ] . The harness-only condition already achieves 99.7 % 99.7\% budget utilization, leaving little room for RL to improve, and the variance in action duration may explain why RL training on MLE-Bench produced negligible gains over the untrained harness. Implementation Details Environment and Interaction Protocol Each turn the model receives the game’s response, a status line [score: s s /350 | moves: m m ] , and the fixed question What is your next action? . It must reply with exactly two lines, a REASONING: line and an ACTION: line (the full template is in the base system prompt, reproduced under Prompts below). Parsing takes the last line beginning with ACTION: ; failing that, the last non-empty line; failing that, the fallback command look . The extracted command is stripped of surrounding quotes and backticks and truncated to 190 190 characters (Jericho truncates commands at 198 198 bytes). A truncated generation therefore never aborts an episode: it silently degrades to look , and the rate of such turns is recorded per configuration. An episode terminates on any of: the agent emitting ACTION: quit (the prompt requires this, so voluntary termination is the intended exit), game over or victory, max_turns = 4000 =4000 , the wall-clock cutoff defined below, a server-side context-length overflow (recorded separately as context_limit ), or an LLM error. Implementation Details: MLE-Bench Agent, Model Serving, and Sandbox The agent is OpenCode 1.17.4, run headless ( opencode run --format json ) with tool calls auto-approved. It uses OpenCode’s built-in tools ( bash , read , write , edit , glob , grep ) and OpenCode’s own system prompt; the task, paths, and budget are the first user message (reproduced under Prompts ). The agent is never given a clock it can call. In every condition it either reads the clock lines the harness appends to tool results or has no clock. Qwen3.6-27B is served by SGLang with tensor parallelism 4 4 and a 131,072 131{,}072 -token context. OpenCode is configured with the same context limit and an output limit of 16,384 16{,}384 tokens per generation, and compacts its history as it nears the limit. A proxy between OpenCode and the inference server records the token ids and log-probabilities of every generation in an episode, with a loss mask that is 1 1 on model-generated tokens and 0 0 on everything the environment authored, including tool results and the clock lines inside them. These records are the training data. Each episode runs in its own Docker container with one dedicated NVIDIA GPU, one episode per container at a time, in a fresh workspace that is deleted afterwards. The competition’s public files are linked into the workspace read-only. The private test labels sit on the same read-only mount and are read by the grader; the prompt tells the agent not to read them, and nothing else prevents it. After every episode, all processes it started are killed before grading, so a background job cannot change submission.csv after the deadline or slow the next episode. Episode, Budget, and Elapsed Time An episode is one OpenCode invocation. It ends when the agent exits or when the harness kills it. In the Table 2 conditions the kill is at 2 ​ B 2B ( 1800 1800 s for the 15 15 -minute budget); the RL run later moved it to B + 30 B+30 s (see Reinforcement Learning ). whatever submission.csv is on disk at that moment is graded. Elapsed time t t is wall clock from the moment the workspace is ready to the moment the agent exits or is killed. It includes generation, tool execution, and harness overhead, and it is the quantity the clock hooks display. The start time is stored in a root-owned file the agent cannot write. The reward takes the larger of the container’s reading and the generator’s own clock, and a failed reading resolves to the cutoff rather than to zero, so no failure can grade as an on-time finish. On budget means t ≤ B t\leq B . Turns is the number of assistant steps in the trajectory, one step being one generation. Valid is the fraction of episodes whose file grades as a valid submission. Grading and Quality After the episode, mlebench.grade.grade_csv grades submission.csv against the private test labels inside the container and returns whether the file is a valid submission (ids, columns, row count, no missing values) and the competition metric. All competitions in the tables are lower-is-better: multi-class log-loss for dog-breed identification, spooky-author identification, and leaf classification; log-loss for dogs-vs-cats; mean column-wise RMSLE for NOMAD 2018. TIME - MEASURE FIRST, THEN CHOOSE EPOCHS: time one epoch, then epochs = (time left - reserve for inference and writing) / measured epoch time. Never pick a round number like 50 up front. If the measurement says your plan can’t finish, cut epochs, image size, or model size immediately - don’t start anyway. - GUARD EVERY LONG COMMAND WITH A TIMEOUT, e.g. ‘timeout 300 python3 train.py‘. Set it shorter than the time remaining shown in the last tool result, with slack to write the submission. Never launch a bare long command: while it blocks you cannot see the clock at all. A hang, or a timeout longer than the time you have left, is the easiest way to lose the whole budget. - Every tool result shows time remaining - re-read it after every call, and work backwards from 15 minutes to the latest moment you can still start writing the submission. - Long generations burn real minutes too. Work in SHORT steps: brief reasoning, brief scripts, run something often. - EXIT ON TIME, WITH REAL PREDICTIONS. The clock stops when you exit, not when you write submission.csv - lingering afterwards still counts as going over. At 15 minutes, stop and exit immediately. Never exit on a copy of sample_submission.csv or uniform values: that scores the same as guessing.
